full_text:
It’s undeniable that playcalling has a massive effect on fantasy football, and that simply picking players on the most efficient offenses creates an edge.

For example, all of the best non-mobile QBs in terms of [greatly exceeding ADP](https://x.com/RyanJ_Heath/status/2015834333660250120?s=20) over the past five years have played in a “McShanahan” system. (That is, under a playcaller who hails from the Sean McVay or Kyle Shanahan coaching tree.) The same goes for finding league-winning passers at the position in the late rounds.

 There are still exactly two paths to success in drafting a QB after Round 10: - Have 100+ rush attempts (Daniels, Maye, Fields) - Play for a "McShanahan" tree playcaller Every late-round QB to make the playoffs in 45%+ of ESPN leagues since 2021 fits one of these two criteria. pic.twitter.com/l7p9gU8oHZ — Ryan Heath (@RyanJ_Heath) July 2, 2026 

Looking beyond the QB position, exactly 50% of league-winning RB/WR/TEs (those with a 55% or better *ESPN* playoff rate) had their plays called by a McShanahan coach or Ben Johnson.

 Since 2022, the "McShanahan" coaching tree plus Ben Johnson have produced 50% of flex-eligible league winners (by ESPN playoff rate). It may not feel like it, but far fewer than 50% of the NFL has played for such a team over this span. Notable overperformance. pic.twitter.com/1Sm7PIlak7 — Ryan Heath (@RyanJ_Heath) July 2, 2026 

__But considering that nearly half the league (44%, to be exact)__ *__is__* __expected to run some version of a “McShanahan” offense in 2026, it’s more important than ever to go beyond coaching tree classification.__ Instead, let’s go under the hood to understand the mechanical reasons many of these offenses succeed (and why others fail). This is where our efficiency hacks come in.

Playcalling Efficiency Hacks To Watch for Fantasy Football
----------------------------------------------------------

As I demonstrated in [last year’s version](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2025/fantasy-football-impact-new-coaches#/) of this article, __play action__ boosts the average WR’s fantasy points per route run (FP/RR) by ~40%, and a TE’s by ~60%. The use of __motion/shift__ was also a potent efficiency hack (+13-16%) in that study.

A new focus for us this year is __during-snap motion__, a subset of those motion plays which drove most of the efficiency gain in 2025; *__a +43% FP/RR increase!__*

 In terms of playcalling cheat codes: During Snap Motion > Pre-Snap Motion > No Motion Last year, skill players saw a 17% YPRR increase on dropbacks with during-snap motion. Or a 43% FP/RR increase! Via: @FantasyPtsData pic.twitter.com/8J846LxhtI — Ryan Heath (@RyanJ_Heath) June 12, 2026 

If we put play action rate and during-snap motion rate (on dropbacks) together on a chart over the past five seasons, we see almost every good playcaller who has provided us outsized fantasy value separate from the pack in one or both. Most of the (successful) McShanahan tree coaches, Ben Johnson, and a few miscellaneous names like Shane Steichen (who just worked a miracle with Daniel Jones), Brian Schottenheimer (who pushed the Cowboys to new fantasy heights), and Todd Monken (who gave us some hyper-efficient Lamar Jackson and Derrick Henry seasons) all stand out.

 It's insane how almost every good NFL playcaller ranks highly in play-action rate, during-snap motion rate, or both. This five-year chart definitely underrates a few guys (i.e., Kubiak has been way higher at times). But a solid snapshot of fantasy value added. @FantasyPtsData pic.twitter.com/EpdlTXDRO1 — Ryan Heath (@RyanJ_Heath) July 2, 2026 

Personnel (i.e., 2-WR vs. 3-WR sets, fullback usage, etc.) is another contributing factor to the fantasy football success and efficiency of several offenses. I wrote [this article on personnel](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2026/finding-the-next-jaxon-smith-njigba-playcaller-tendencies#/) earlier in the offseason. It’s an incredibly important piece of the playcaller puzzle; WRs see a ~32% per-route efficiency boost with two or fewer WRs on the field compared to plays with three or more, and playcaller history can help us identify teams and receivers who could benefit from this cheat code. Last year’s [version of this article](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2025/fantasy-football-impact-new-coaches) mentioned this angle for then-Seahawks OC Klint Kubiak and Jaxon Smith-Njigba, the biggest WR breakout of the season.

![](STATIC_ASSET_URI/photos/c39309d1931f54ef72e3ad2eb2501a955e39ea6e/388a348d484c6b6efd50e06816f8b503511dbf6e)

But half the reason I wrote about personnel back in May of this year was to free up space to focus on literally everything else in today’s article. So if that’s what you’re looking for, you’ll find it linked above (and throughout this article, wherever we touch on a relevant point).

Now, let’s put all these efficiency hacks together to evaluate all 18 new team/playcaller combinations for the 2026 season. I’ll also bring in any other historical tendencies (pass rates, backfield utilization, pace of play, etc.) that might give us an edge at predicting which players will benefit in fantasy football. __And new this year, I’ll be providing a TL;DR at the top of each section indicating whether I’m positive, mixed, or neutral on each playcaller and applicable player.__

But first, let’s briefly touch on a few fantasy-relevant angles involving returning playcallers.

General Trends and Fantasy Notes On Returning Playcallers
---------------------------------------------------------

+ __For full clarity, I’d consider the 49ers, Rams, Packers, Vikings, Dolphins, Texans, Jaguars, Bengals, Cardinals, Chargers, Raiders, Eagles, Seahawks, and Buccaneers offenses to have “McShanahan” tree playcallers entering 2026.__ We’ll cover him later, but Sean Mannion of the Eagles is an edge case; he’s never actually coached with McVay or Shanahan (my usual inclusion criteria). But he did play under McVay from 2017-2018 and coached with his disciple Matt LaFleur for two seasons, so I chose to count him.

+ We learned that Vikings HC __Kevin O’Connell__ has a limit as a “QB whisperer” last year; J.J. McCarthy and Max Brosmer were [simply too unequipped](https://x.com/RyanJ_Heath/status/2055358911390117952?s=20) to allow his offense to succeed. But that hasn’t been true of all manner of journeyman QBs and marginal talents he’s had pass through over the years. Nick Mullens, Joshua Dobbs, and Carson Wentz have averaged 18.1 FPG under O’Connell across 12 full games. The fact that his offenses have ranked top-5 in pass rate inside the 10-yard line over each of the past three seasons also speaks to the fantasy-friendliness. So long as you believe that __Kyler Murray__ is at least as good as Mullens, Dobbs, and Wentz ([as I do](https://x.com/RyanJ_Heath/status/2055358912858091730?s=20)) and have optimism about Murray’s ability under-center, he’s clearly one of the highest-upside late-round QBs available.

 Since 2021, Kyler Murray's Cardinals rank 4th-highest in shotgun rate (71.8%) The Vikings ranked bottom-3 every year from 2021-24. Even in 2025 with Wentz/McCarthy, they ranked 8th-lowest (48.2%). However, Murray has been more efficient from under center! Via @FantasyPtsData pic.twitter.com/ORSd1C1NiM — Ryan Heath (@RyanJ_Heath) June 2, 2026 

+ With __Travis Etienne__ on the move from Jacksonville to New Orleans, I expect he’ll see fewer designed screen targets. Saints HC __Kellen Moore__ ranks 6th-lowest in total designed targets per game, while Jaguars HC Liam Coen ranks 3rd-highest. And Moore specifically avoids giving them to his backfield; the only Kellen Moore RB to ever average more than 0.75 designed targets per game was Austin Ekeler (none of Tony Pollard, Saquon Barkley, or Alvin Kamara were deemed worthy). For comparison, Etienne just averaged 2.5 FPG on 1.3 designed targets/game under Coen.

![](STATIC_ASSET_URI/photos/c39309d1931f54ef72e3ad2eb2501a955e39ea6e/c5ef02d42a917cd5da1d7ddc907e3f20da6fee2b)

+ For years, we’ve bemoaned Packers HC __Matt LaFleur’s__ “WR by committee.” Since 2023, no Packers WR aside from Romeo Doubs ever crested a 70% route share in any season, with the rest of his pass-catchers caught in fantasy football upside-destroying snap rotations (For perspective, 34 of the 36 WR/TEs to average 16.0+ FPG in a season over that span saw at least a 70% route share.) But now, LaFleur himself has [suggested](https://youtu.be/n_tx3A3mR7g?si=RjyYPCp_txNOb4J2) he’ll have an easier time giving his star players more opportunities after the departures of Doubs and Dontayvion Wicks. Even if we get a handful of __Savion Williams__ snaps each game that nobody asked for, players like __Christian Watson__ and __J____ayden Reed__ should easily set career-highs in route share this year. Watson averages 17.5 FPG (~WR6) across 13 career games above a 75% route share! (And even Reed averages a usable 14.2 FPG in 12 career games above 70%.)

+ All this said, I’m quite afraid that HC __Liam Coen’s__ Jaguars could end up as “Packers South” this year. Top Jaguars beat writer John Shipley seems to think similarly, [noting](https://www.si.com/nfl/jaguars/onsi/jacksonville-debunking-3-overreactions-from-offseason-patience-key-wr) the team has four exciting WRs and that the best years of Trevor Lawrence’s career came in seasons he spread the ball around. Nobody [quite seems to know](https://x.com/DhananiZain/status/2071408148540162310?s=20) which of __Parker Washington__ or __Brian Thomas Jr.__ will come off the field for Travis Hunter — could a [part-time](https://x.com/RyanJ_Heath/status/2054289358023242034?s=20) [30-40% route share](https://x.com/DhananiZain/status/2075007429851431395?s=20) for him destroy the fantasy viability of one or both, just as Dontayvion Wicks did to the Packers? This is further complicated by the (in my view, very small) chance the Jaguars use more multi-TE sets as James Gladstone [seems to desire](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2026/finding-the-next-jaxon-smith-njigba-playcaller-tendencies#/) (I’d easily back Coen to win that power struggle). I’m more open to Washington’s upside in the slot (below), but Coen also [notably transitioned](https://x.com/RyanJ_Heath/status/2070576975689687479?s=20) Thomas into a much deeper and less fantasy-friendly role as last season went on, and it sounds like [that isn’t changing](https://x.com/BGWhitefield/status/2069807959362732201?s=20).

 Liam Coen's slot WRs, a history: 2021: 102.6 receiving YPG from Wan'Dale Robinson at Kentucky 2022: 22.4 FPG from Cooper Kupp (~WR1) 2024: 19.7 FPG from Chris Godwin (~WR2) 2025: 17.5 FPG from Parker Washington in 8 healthy post-bye games (incl. playoffs) pic.twitter.com/l51lNASlIG — Ryan Heath (@RyanJ_Heath) July 2, 2026 

+ But Coen is so great that taking shots on his WRs (with an understanding of the low floor and uncertainty) could still be worth it (particularly if Washington remains available as just a fringe top-100 pick on home league platforms). Since 2021, Coen ranks 3rd-best among all playcallers in EPA/play (0.15), behind only Todd Monken and Kyle Shanahan, and ahead of Andy Reid and Ben Johnson. He ranks 7th by yards per play (6.31) and 1st in points per game (28.7). So I am ultimately going to draft a lot of Washington, and much more concretely, anything one could say about Coen’s impact on __Trevor Lawrence__ or __Bhayshul Tuten__ is overwhelmingly positive.

 Top active playcallers by QB FPG since 2021 1. Joe Brady - 22.5 2. Liam Coen - 21.7 3. Todd Monken - 21.2 4. Zac Taylor - 20.5 5. Andy Reid - 20.4 Coen w/ Baker Mayfield and Trevor Lawrence has outdone the guys with Josh Allen, Lamar Jackson, Joe Burrow, and Patrick Mahomes. pic.twitter.com/1BtvKuXPQw — Fantasy Points Data (@FantasyPtsData) June 20, 2026 

 Leading playcallers by total backfield fantasy volume (XFP/G) over the past 3 seasons [min. 20 games] 1. Kyle Shanahan - 26.4 2. Mike McDaniel - 26.2 3. Ben Johnson - 25.6 4. Zac Robinson - 25.2 5. Arthur Smith - 25.2 6. Sean Payton - 24.0 7. Liam Coen - 23.3 @FantasyPtsData — Ryan Heath (@RyanJ_Heath) May 19, 2026 

+ Just to underscore the value of Coen’s offense with a third bullet point, only four current playcallers rank above the median in *both* dropbacks per game and fantasy points per dropback over the past five seasons. (It’s hard to maintain both a high-volume and high-efficiency passing attack.) Every other team to whom this applies (the Cowboys, Bengals, and Chiefs) have multiple players being selected inside the first four rounds of ADP. The first Jaguar off the board is RB Bhayshul Tuten in Round 5 at the earliest. No member of their passing game gets selected until Round 6. There’s ambiguity as to who will receive the volume, but there’s immense fantasy value to be had if you pick correctly.

![](STATIC_ASSET_URI/photos/c39309d1931f54ef72e3ad2eb2501a955e39ea6e/5b4e886aa38ec45264ccc23ae47269ca4c76309b)

+ Per *The Athletic*, __Joe Burrow__ and the Bengals [could be planning](https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/7387460/2026/06/24/bengals-offense-under-center-joe-burrow/) to use more under-center play action this year. Burrow is one of the very few QBs who *doesn’*t have notably positive efficiency splits on these plays since 2021 [1] , but interestingly, __Tee Higgins__ (3.36 YPRR) has been much more productive and efficient than __Ja’Marr Chase__ (1.85 YPRR) on such dropbacks since 2021. And regardless, it remains crazy to me that Higgins averages 17.5 FPG (~WR6) in Burrow’s starts over the past two seasons, yet is drafted well behind that. I want to draft Higgins more with every day that passes.

+ And as Jared Smola illustrates below, playing under center can also have a positive impact on the run game, great news for __Chase Brown__. Brown averaged 21.0 FPG (~RB5) in games Burrow started and finished last year. He’s a killer Round 2 target.

 Bengals planning more under center play-action plays this year. Good news for the passing game ... but also Chase Brown. https://t.co/Puyps9Cl5f pic.twitter.com/kgHD06vWye — Jared Smola (@SmolaDS) June 25, 2026 

+ Horizontally breaking routes are another [efficiency hack](https://x.com/RyanJ_Heath/status/2071717007339278727?s=20) we haven’t yet discussed. Patriots OC __Josh McDaniels__ deployed them to great effect with Stefon Diggs last year, who ran them at the 12th-highest rate (42.8%) and averaged the most YPRR (3.77) on them of any qualifying WR. New Patriots WR1 __A.J. Brown__ hasn’t run horizontal-breakers as often over the past four seasons (37.9%), but his 3.20 YPRR on them ranks best of any WR over that span. Now in a potentially perfect role/skillset match and with __Drake Maye__ as his QB, we shouldn’t be surprised if Brown has his most productive fantasy season yet.

 Here's where A.J. Brown's teams have ranked in passing yards ... 2019: 21st 2020: 23rd 2021: 24th 2022: 9th 2023: 16th 2024: 29th 2025: 23rd ------------ 2025 Patriots: 4th — Jared Smola (@SmolaDS) June 2, 2026 

New Playcallers
---------------

![](STATIC_ASSET_URI/photos/c39309d1931f54ef72e3ad2eb2501a955e39ea6e/3743baff17a31fa326f8789f15144ed53ff6ad3b)

__Arizona Cardinals__
---------------------

##### Mike LaFleur replaces Drew Petzing

###### __Positive:__ Marvin Harrison Jr.

###### __Mixed:__ Mike LaFleur, Trey McBride, Jeremiyah Love

###### __Negative:__ Michael Wilson

The brother of Packers HC Matt LaFleur finally gets his own chance to lead a team this year, after having called plays as the Jets’ OC from 2021-22 and spending time coaching under both Kyle Shanahan and Sean McVay on each end of that stint.

It doesn’t get much more “McShanahan” than that by pedigree, but it’s entirely debatable whether LaFleur’s past results and cheat code usage live up to that label. His overall dropback efficiency (4.99 ANY/A) ranks dead-last of all 25 current playcallers to have called 10+ games over the past five years. His dropback motion (50.3%,17th) and play-action (25.3%, 21st) rates are both solidly below average for that span, too.

![](STATIC_ASSET_URI/photos/c39309d1931f54ef72e3ad2eb2501a955e39ea6e/faac4f5beab70cc582f2100bf0f0c92637eeab35)

So we definitely shouldn’t go crazy; the younger LaFleur’s overall track record is not strong, and I’m not expecting high-end efficiency with this roster. But in fairness to him, the stats above largely reflect an offense led by Zach Wilson, who [remained just as horrible an efficiency black hole](https://x.com/FantasyPtsData/status/2064750269447967209?s=20) in 2023, after LaFleur left.

When we attempt to control for Wilson, we can paint a more compelling upside picture for the passing offense. __Across 12 Mike White and Joe Flacco starts, LaFleur’s Jets averaged 305.5 passing YPG, which would have led the NFL last year.__ That happened largely because LaFleur was willing to unleash a high-volume pass attack into negative game scripts. __His 60.6% pass rate ranks 6th-highest among all playcallers with a full season or more to their name since 2021__, and he ranked top-6 in pace in both years with the Jets.

I’m sure that airing it out isn’t LaFleur’s intention: this team’s top two free agent contracts went to a guard (Isaac Seumalo) and an RB (__Tyler Allgeier__), as did their top two draft picks (RB __Jeremiyah Love__ and G Chase Bisontis). But the Cardinals have just a 4.5 win total over/under, and added no splashy free agents and no Day 1 or Day 2 draft picks to a defense that allowed the 4th-most points and the 7th-most EPA/play last year. LaFleur even retained DC Nick Rallis — this unit was admittedly decimated by injuries in 2025, but that’s really the only variable playing in their favor.

This is all mostly to say there’s still a world in which __Jacoby Brissett__ (or __Gardner Minshew__) could lead the NFL in dropbacks per start out of necessity, just as he did last year (45.8). Brissett averaged 19.9 FPG over this span (~QB7).

I’ve also previously thrown cold water on Cardinals’ pass-catchers like __Trey McBride__ (21.1 FPG with Brissett, would rank most by any TE ever) and __Michael Wilson__ (16.8 FPG with Brissett, ~WR9) for having accumulated most of their production in garbage time. McBride even ran [roughly 22 games](https://x.com/LordReebs/status/2069782818016682122?s=20) worth of routes last year!

 Most targets when trailing by multiple scores in the 4th quarter [2025, @FantasyPtsData ] 1. Trey McBride - 26 2. Michael Wilson - 25 3. Harold Fannin - 22 4. Ja'Marr Chase - 22 5. Rashid Shaheed - 22 — Ryan Heath (@RyanJ_Heath) January 26, 2026 

But, indulge me. *__What if the Cardinals continue to fall behind every game, and LaFleur just lets his offense do the same thing they did last year, and that White and Flacco did under him with the Jets?__* It probably won’t happen to the same extent that created the production referenced above — in 2025, Arizona’s 69.5% pass rate was the most by any offense in the *Fantasy Points Data* era — but what if I’m saying you *are* allowed to think of this as a high-volume passing offense just on the off-chance?

Well, __Marvin Harrison Jr.__ would become an interesting [Year 3 breakout](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2024/age-curves-when-nfl-players-break-out) bet on [one of the best WR prospects of the past decade](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2024/pre-nfl-draft-rookie-wr-dynasty-rankings) at an ADP outside the first five rounds. Harrison averaged 14.9 FPG (~WR11) on 18.7 XFP/G (~WR4) in three full games with Brissett, commanding a higher first-read target share (38.0%, ~WR4) than McBride (36.6%) in those contests.

My point is not that any of these examples are the most likely outcome, but rather that insane negative gamescript-fueled dropback volume is much more in play to me than I expected it to be, after examining LaFleur’s history.

So ultimately, I only really believe this upside case as it pertains to Harrison, whose pedigree and chance to play under a McShanahan playcaller creates a non garbage time-related path to paying off big at cost. McBride is both much more expensive and might specifically need Brissett’s [absurdly high career TE target rate](https://x.com/FantasyPts/status/2072636503100936270?s=20) (the Cardinals could easily start all three of Brissett, Minshew, and rookie __Carson Beck__ at different points this year). I’m also not as into Wilson for the reasons [laid out here](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2026/finding-the-next-jaxon-smith-njigba-playcaller-tendencies#/) (TL;DR, he did most of his damage from cheat-code heavy personnel and/or without Harrison on the field, neither of which I expect to continue).

My thoughts on the backfield are much simpler. I personally trust LaFleur’s taste in running backs after [how he handled](https://x.com/RyanJ_Heath/status/2064721589329866873?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw) a rookie Breece Hall and am [not that worried](https://x.com/RyanJ_Heath/status/2047495013316087849?s=20) about a committee with Tyler Allgeier, but Love’s ADP near the Round 2/3 turn isn’t enough of a discount for that uncertainty to me when we’re talking about an RB on a team with a 4.5 win total. So I’m open to a strong rookie season from Love, but he isn’t a priority redraft target to me.

__Atlanta Falcons__
-------------------

##### Tommy Rees replaces Zac Robinson

###### __Positive:__ Bijan Robinson

###### __Mixed:__ Tommy Rees, Kyle Pitts

New Falcons HC Kevin Stefanski brings OC Tommy Rees with him to Atlanta to serve as the primary playcaller. I’d called out Rees as a TE-whisperer in [last year’s article](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2025/fantasy-football-impact-new-coaches#/), and he ultimately took over playcalling duties for the Browns midway through 2025.

It definitely isn’t fair to judge Rees’s overall results on depleted offenses helmed by Shedeur Sanders and Dillon Gabriel. Neither he nor Stefanski’s sample of games in 2025 broke out of the bottom-5 playcallers by either yards per play or points per drive, so I wouldn’t bank on Rees elevating this offense above and beyond its talent level (which, to be fair, is *much* higher than that of the Browns). Still, he does have some particular tendencies we can discuss and target.

As a refresher, Michael Mayer and Tommy Tremble combined for over a 25% target share in Rees’s first season as OC at Notre Dame, despite the presence of future NFL talents Kyren Williams and Ben Skowronek. Mayer led the team with 23% and 32% target shares over Rees’ next two seasons, ending his college career with [historically great raw production](https://x.com/ScottBarrettDFB/status/1783675247910162838?s=20). Rees didn’t have notable TE usage as OC at Alabama in 2023, but he did manage to help Jalen Milroe average the 2nd-highest YPA in the NCAA that year (10.0). Finally and most recently, Rees was promoted to Browns OC in 2025, when Harold Fannin scored the 5th-most PPR points by any rookie TE since the merger (186.4, behind only Brock Bowers, Sam LaPorta, Keith Jackson, and Tyler Warren).

That all sounds encouraging for __Kyle Pitts__, as does Rees’s [expected personnel usage](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2026/finding-the-next-jaxon-smith-njigba-playcaller-tendencies#/). But this is only barely enough to justify Pitts as not *actively awful* at ADP; Pitts averaged just 10.0 FPG (~TE17) with __Drake London__ in the lineup, and his first-read target share on intermediate routes was [cut by more than half](https://x.com/FantasyKash/status/2064116271369556155?s=20) with London vs. without him. I honestly don’t want to draft Pitts at all, despite the playcaller tendency I’m obligated to point out here.

But with __Bijan Robinson__ a consensus top-2 fantasy pick, let’s turn to the backfield.

Robinson ranked tied with Deebo Samuel for the most [designed targets](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2025/statistically-significant-designed-targets#/) in the NFL last year (30). Since these can be very playcaller-dependent, I wanted to take a look at Rees’s designed target usage, and I came away encouraged. Not only does Rees’s 8.74 yards per designed target average rank best of any 2026 playcaller, but he also utilized them slightly more than former OC Zac Robinson did overall. __And after Rees took over playcalling in Week 10,__ __65% of the Browns’ designed targets went to RBs (compared to 46% with Stefanski calling plays).__ All of Quinshon Judkins, Dylan Sampson, and Trayveon Williams averaged over 8.0 yards per designed target with Rees.

![](STATIC_ASSET_URI/photos/c39309d1931f54ef72e3ad2eb2501a955e39ea6e/c5ef02d42a917cd5da1d7ddc907e3f20da6fee2b)

So I expect Robinson to build even further upon his [historically amazing](https://x.com/RyanJ_Heath/status/2064418555047608591?s=20) receiving role from last year, and likely Falcons Week 1 starter __Tua Tagovailoa__ owns the [highest RB target rate](https://x.com/FantasyPts/status/2073029283778376147?s=20) in the NFL over the past two years. We can definitely nitpick his fit as a runner in Rees’s scheme as I’ve done in this footnote, [2] but that’s ultimately just a tie-breaker to make him my 1.02 after Jahmyr Gibbs (whom we’ll discuss even more bullishly below).

__Baltimore Ravens__
--------------------

##### Declan Doyle replaces Todd Monken

###### __Positive:__ Declan Doyle, Derrick Henry, Lamar Jackson, Zay Flowers

Doyle came up as an offensive assistant with Sean Payton’s Saints, and followed Payton to Denver in 2023. Bears HC Ben Johnson hired Doyle as his OC in 2025, and now the 30-year-old will get to call plays for the first time in Baltimore.

It’s going to be pretty hard for Doyle to outdo outgoing OC Todd Monken’s [efficiency and accomplishments](https://x.com/RyanJ_Heath/status/2065534512650478010?s=20) in Baltimore. But I’m weirdly bullish. Zay Flowers [calls](https://x.com/giana_jade/status/2061886401717617101?s=20) Doyle a “genius,” while Lamar Jackson [says](https://www.baltimoreravens.com/news/lamar-jackson-declan-doyle-cursing-out-mind-blowing-details-methods-coaching-style-mandatory-camp-2026) he’s “mind-blowing.” *ESPN* [notes](https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/48958657/baltimore-ravens-2026-nfl-offensive-coordinator-declan-doyle-reboot-offense) that his motion and shift usage in summer practices has caused long conversations among the Ravens’ defensive coaches, so that’s one playcalling cheat code checked off.

As for the other cheat code (play action), Johnson and Payton are two of the better influences one could ask for. Johnson’s Bears ranked 2nd in the NFL in play-action dropback rate last year (35.0%), while the Broncos ranked 10th when Doyle was with them in 2024 (29.0%). Johnson has even used play-action at a top-three rate among all playcallers over the past five seasons (32.3%, behind only Mike McDaniel and Shane Steichen).

There’s no guarantee Doyle does the same, but he did [credit](https://x.com/CHGO_Bears/status/1993408418720497913?s=20) Caleb Williams’ improvement on play action as important to the Bears’ offense last year. From this, we might infer that play action is on Doyle’s mind as a big piece of his offense.

__Lamar Jackson__ is statistically the NFL’s best play-action passer over the past two seasons (he’s even [more accurate](https://x.com/BGWhitefield/status/2072670318229954620?s=20) on play action!), but he ranked just 20th in play-action dropback rate last year. The Seahawks’ offense under incoming OC Brian Fleury has proven the hardest to write about of any on this very long list.

Fleury has been on Kyle Shanahan’s staff in San Francisco since 2019, most recently holding the titles of tight ends coach and run game coordinator. So the McShanahan DNA will still technically run through Seattle this season, but Fleury has never called an offense at any level of football and was a defensive/special-teams coach for most of his career before linking up with Shanahan. We’re left guessing at what his playcalling tendencies could look like.

And the Seahawks aren’t giving us many hints. __Sam Darnold__ says Fleury’s offense [doesn’t require](https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/48961312/seahawks-sam-darnold-sees-little-transition-brian-fleury-offense) much of a transition, while Fleury says it “looks very similar to the one that just won the Super Bowl.” Maybe this isn’t at all fair of me, but this all gives me a [similar vibe](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2025/fantasy-football-impact-new-coaches#/) to how I felt reading about Kevin Patullo’s offense last summer with the Eagles coming off their Super Bowl win.

The best macro-level nugget I could find was from Seahawks insider Gregg Bell, who [reported the offense](https://youtu.be/JUYM9Pi0vR8?si=RIV_-DZYiaOx3akt&t=1192) is using a lot more slip motion around when the ball was snapped (i.e., something we’d chart as “during-snap motion”) based on his observations of early June practices. Jeremy Fowler recently [confirmed something similar](https://x.com/JFowlerESPN/status/2071302126450405518?s=20). That would be a meaningful change; __Jaxon Smith-Njigba__ ran only 69 routes on such plays last year (57th among WRs/TEs).

![](STATIC_ASSET_URI/photos/c39309d1931f54ef72e3ad2eb2501a955e39ea6e/5b417580e0b60a3f1a740148e72aa51939f46f2f)

But it’s also not clear this would help him, as it’s pretty hard to be *more* efficient than Smith-Njigba was last year, and his YPRR actually slightly declined with during-snap motion (3.64 vs. 3.74 on all routes). And that’s the theme I keep coming back to with the Seahawks; *e**ven if Fleury uses all the right playcalling cheat codes and maximizes every edge, is it reasonable to expect the offense to come close to last year’s efficiency?*

If not, that’s a problem. For example, Smith-Njigba saw very low red zone usage for a high-end fantasy WR last year.

The group averaged 1.45. JSN averaged exactly 1.0 red zone target per game in 2025. https://t.co/emZwBKTP1m — Ryan Heath (@RyanJ_Heath) July 1, 2026 

Fewer red zone targets aren’t a surprise — remember, Klint Kubiak was [ultra-run-heavy near the goal line](https://x.com/fball_insights/status/2055001356872581346?s=20) — but Fleury sounds like he’ll be similar or even more run-heavy. Via the [CoachSpeak Index](https://x.com/CoachspeakIndex) Discord, Fleury believes “the people that can run it in the red zone have the most success,” and wants to have “the dynamic run game down there, and different ways to attack people more horizontally than vertically, just because the field is wider than it is shorter down there.”

That’s a reasonable real-life approach, but it is a blow to Smith-Njigba’s fantasy prospects if the Seahawks can’t be expected to throw more in the red zone (and perhaps a boon to __Zach Charbonnet__’s and __Jadarian Price__’s, especially if Charbonnet is [progressing well](https://x.com/JFowlerESPN/status/2071583707865981026?s=20)). Last year, Smith-Njigba made up the difference via hyper-efficiency on the deep ball. How repeatable is that? Let’s investigate.

For starters, __Sam Darnold’s 52.1% highly accurate throw rate on attempts of 20+ yards downfield ranks 1st of 149 qualifying QB seasons in the__ *__Fantasy Points Data__* __era.__ That may sound like an overly specific stat, but Smith-Njigba scored 92.9 fantasy points on these plays (the most in the NFL, and the 6th-most by any player since 2021). That’s nearly 26% of his fantasy point total on the season scored on only 16 targets where things fell *just right*. (And, to relate this back to Kubiak, half of *those* targets utilized deep play action, his [special sauce](https://x.com/RyanJ_Heath/status/2069484199287910585?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw).)

So I’m expecting regression. Of the 21 WRs with next-season data to score 60.0+ fantasy points on highly accurate deep balls, they averaged 36.6 fantasy points on them the next season (roughly half the original-season average of 78.9). Only three of the 21 matched their previous-season total.

To ground all this back in terms of total fantasy scoring, the group saw roughly a 2.3 FPG decline (from an average of 16.6 to 14.3). 16 of the 21 players (76%) who were this fortunate on highly accurate deep targets averaged fewer FPG the following season. And it was all this efficiency that allowed Smith-Njigba to average 21.2 FPG on just 16.2 XFP/G last year (making him the ~WR7 by volume). His +5.0 FPOE was tied for the 5th-most by a WR in the *Fantasy Points Data* era.

This is all mostly just to say that it’s going to take more than some slip motion in June to convince me that Fleury (or any first-time playcaller; the impossibility of his task really isn’t his fault) is going to get as strong of results on as low of pass volume as Kubiak did. Of the five other seasons a WR has hit 5.0+ FPOE, Kyle Shanahan and Sean McVay themselves are responsible for four. Smith-Njigba hit the pinnacle of WR efficiency for the first time under Kubiak, and the more I dig into it, the less I want to bet he’ll do the same under a new unknown OC at a top-5 overall ADP, with a now highly paid and [likely more involved](https://x.com/JFowlerESPN/status/2071302126450405518?s=20) __Rashid Shaheed__ to boot.

So this all gets tied together perfectly once I tell you that __Godwin ranks 3rd in YPRR on plays with during-snap motion over the past two seasons (3.99, behind only Puka Nacua and Nico Collins),__ *__including 2nd in 2025 alone (4.02) despite playing injured.__* Oh, and Robinson [talks to Liam Coen every day](https://www.si.com/nfl/buccaneers/onsi/news/zac-robinson-opens-up-about-relationship-with-former-buccaneers-oc-liam-coen-2026).

There’s certainly a chance that Godwin has nothing left in the tank at this point in his career, and during-snap motion did also help __Emeka Egbuka__, even if to a lesser extent (2.41 YPRR). And I don’t want to lose sight of the fact that Robinson [compared](https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/48771161/2026-nfl-offseason-big-questions-second-year-sophomore-players-2025-draft) Egbuka to Cooper Kupp this offseason, saying they’re similar “in terms of the way that his brain works with the game of football and natural instincts.” Kupp produced 1,947 receiving yards (the 2nd-most by any WR ever) on 191 targets (13th-most ever) in his last fully healthy season with Robinson on the Rams’ staff in 2021.

So I’m not entirely sure which one it will be, but I am confident that one of Egbuka or Godwin will break leagues this year. Draft accordingly!

As for the running backs, Robinson ranks 2nd-best among active playcallers in backfield XFP/G (28.0, behind only Ben Johnson), 6th in rush attempts per game (28.6), and has been [one of the most](https://x.com/fball_insights/status/2055001356872581346?s=20) run-heavy playcallers inside the 10-yard line. Mayfield himself [has remarked](https://www.buccaneers.com/news/baker-mayfield-sees-retooled-offense-zac-robinson-2026-bucs-blitz) that he’s excited for Robinson’s offense to [open up more for him via the run game](https://www.buccaneers.com/news/baker-mayfield-sees-retooled-offense-zac-robinson-2026-bucs-blitz). But he likens that to 2024, when the Buccaneers still ranked top-12 in dropbacks per game (38.4), while Robinson’s Falcons ranked bottom-10 in each of his two seasons.

So I don’t want to assume that Robinson’s 2026 Buccaneers will be as run-heavy as his Falcons squads were, when he had a backfield led by Bijan Robinson and a combination of Michael Penix and a late-30s Kirk Cousins off an Achilles tear under center. The backfield will likely not be as valuable overall, and none of the Buccaneers’ RBs are obvious rushing scheme fits for him.

This isn’t so much to say that the run game will fail, as it is to point out that __Bucky Irving__’s previous efficiency (particularly from 2024) may not prove predictive of whether he’ll run away with the work in *this* backfield. Robinson has [described his backfield approach](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2026/heaths-favorite-best-ball-values#/) as “feeling the hot hand, we’ll see where it goes.”

But one thing that *could* translate from Robinson’s prior offenses is the fact that he’s liked to concentrate screen targets with his RBs rather than with his WRs; Bijan led the NFL in screen targets last year (30), and ranks top-5 in designed target share among all players over Robinson’s tenure with the Falcons. That was despite the presence of other viable speed/screen threats on the team like Ray-Ray McCloud and Darnell Mooney.

So, much of the intrigue in the Buccaneers’ backfield for me centers around which of Irving or __Kenneth Gainwell__ will see the most designed screen work (and receiving work in general). Gainwell won the most screen targets (19) compared to backfield mate Jaylen Warren (9) in 2025, but in 2024, screens in Liam Coen’s offense gave Irving [a meaningful boost](https://x.com/RyanJ_Heath/status/1915840449815650417?s=20). Again, this backfield is quite ambiguous.

__Tennessee Titans__
--------------------

##### Brian Daboll replaces Brian Callahan/Bo Hardegree

###### __Mixed:__ Tony Pollard

###### __Negative:__ Brian Daboll, Cam Ward

Daboll is a weird playcaller to evaluate, but I’ve always felt his reputation has outpaced his results. He’s long been credited for the early development of Josh Allen, but especially with the benefit of hindsight as to what Allen has accomplished without Daboll (better efficiency and an MVP award) and to what Daboll has accomplished without Allen (little), I don’t really buy that.

 Josh Allen's ANY/A by season: 2018: 4.37 2019: 5.71 2020: 7.81 2021: 6.38 *Brian Daboll leaves* 2022: 6.99 2023: 6.51 2024: 7.96 2025: 6.84 Allen has been more efficient than in Daboll's final year each of the past four seasons, including two without Stefon Diggs/a star WR1. — Ryan Heath (@RyanJ_Heath) July 1, 2026 

We got another QB efficiency case study with Daniel Jones. Shane Steichen is legitimately great (and an actual QB whisperer), but I’m going to go ahead and say it’s bad if your playcaller is less efficient than Jason Garrett. Even Daboll’s own OC (Mike Kafka) outperformed him.

 Daniel Jones' ANY/A by playcaller since 2021 Shane Steichen - 7.30 Freddie Kitchens - 6.90 (one-game sample) Jason Garrett - 5.51 Mike Kafka (with Daboll as HC) - 5.03 "QB whisperer" Brian Daboll - 4.71 @FantasyPtsData — Ryan Heath (@RyanJ_Heath) July 1, 2026 

Since 2021, Daboll has utilized play-action at the 2nd-highest rate out of our new playcallers (29.1%, behind only Mike McDaniel), or 8th-most among all 2026 playcallers. But that isn’t a *ton* more than __Cam Ward__ used as a rookie (24.9% of his dropbacks), and Ward’s play-action ANY/A (5.99) was already better than 2025 Jaxson Dart’s (4.43) and 2024 Daniel Jones’ (5.59), so I don’t see that as a massive area of potential improvement, either.

So no, I haven’t found good statistical evidence to suggest Daboll will boost Ward’s play to a fantasy-relevant extent. And this ultimately means I don’t have any particular interest in the Titans’ passing game for managed redraft leagues.

I only have two relevant (though low-confidence) notes on the backfield. The first is that while Daboll’s teams have been all over the map by rushing scheme, over the last five years, the two teams for which he’s actually called the plays (the 2021 Bills and 2024 Giants) ranked 9th (50.8%) and 12th (47.6%) in backfield man/gap carry rate. Since arriving in Tennessee, __Tony Pollard__ has been notably more efficient on man/gap carries (4.29) than __Tyjae Spears__ (3.59), while they’ve been closer (4.34 vs. 4.15 YPC) by zone concept efficiency.

So perhaps that helps Pollard maintain his hold on the rushing workload. But I also don’t think it should be lost on us that Daboll has [only ever given](https://x.com/RyanJ_Heath/status/2072452476498776437?s=20) 200 or more carries to elite talents. For comparison, Pollard has surpassed 240 over each of the past three seasons.

__Washington Commanders__
-------------------------

##### David Blough replaces Kliff Kingsbury

###### __Positive:__ Jayden Daniels, Terry McLaurin, Jacory Croskey-Merritt

###### __Mixed:__ David Blough

*ESPN’s* John Keim [reported as early as January](https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/47528237/sources-kingsbury-whitt-commanders-coordinators) that Commanders HC Dan Quinn has his own vision for the Commanders’ offense moving forward, and a conflicting one with outgoing OC Kliff Kingsbury, at that. Per Keim, Quinn wanted to “run the ball more to control the clock and help the defense,” while he was suspicious of Kingsbury’s heavy no-huddle approach.

My initial instinct was that a power struggle like that followed by the Commanders going with an internal OC hire in David Blough — a former QB whose coaching experience starts and stops at being the team’s assistant QB coach over the past two seasons — should raise alarm bells. We’re obviously working off limited information, but Quinn feels far too involved, and it seems odd on its face that the Commanders didn’t attract a bigger name to come and work with __Jayden Daniels__.

Maybe I’m foolish to ignore my first impression. But the more I learn about Blough, the more I’m intrigued, and the more I think this will actually work out well for the Commanders’ skill players in fantasy football. (I really only have him in the “mixed” category because of the Dan Quinn of it all.)

Supposedly, the Commanders hired Blough [to stave off an advance](https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/49166861/new-nfl-coordinators-offense-defense-questions-2026-season-cowboys-bills-commanders) from the Lions seeking to fill their OC job. Both Kingsbury (who originally recruited him to Washington) and Ben Johnson (under whom he played) have [glowing things to say about him](https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/49166861/new-nfl-coordinators-offense-defense-questions-2026-season-cowboys-bills-commanders), including predictions that he’ll move up quickly and become a head coach.

Blough himself has also said all the right things this offseason. He [plans](https://www.commanders.com/news/washington-commanders-offensive-coordinator-david-blough-top-quotes) to get Daniels under center more, and appreciated Kingsbury’s ability to use tempo to put stress on defenses. He has Quinn’s support (below) on the former idea, and as I explained in [this earlier piece](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2026/fantasy-football-qb-stats-what-matters#/), any disagreements Quinn and his playcaller may have about pace of play seem unlikely to negatively impact Daniels’ fantasy production relative to last year.

 HC Dan Quinn said Commanders offense under new OC David Blough will feature more under center and play action. — Underdog NFL (@UnderdogNFL) February 10, 2026 

__Daniels has even scrambled more when playing under center or from the pistol (21.3% scramble rate) than from the shotgun (12.0%).__ [11] And like most QBs, he enjoyed a boost in his ANY/A (in his case, +21%) on play action last season. The latter probably won’t make a huge difference to the offense (the Commanders have already ranked top-5 in play action dropback rate over each of the past two seasons), but getting under center more will be a major change (89% of Daniels’ career dropbacks have come from the shotgun).

But Blough is arguably even more bullish for __Terry McLaurin__, who he wants to build the offense around [and to whom he’d like to direct](https://x.com/SleeperNFL/status/2022002012599332973?s=20) 10 targets per game. More target volume would be massive; __over the past two seasons, McLaurin is the WR10 by FP/RR (0.51) but just the WR32 by TPRR (0.23).__

Even if you take the target number with a grain of salt, the attitude is directionally encouraging, and there are no shortage of other reasons to believe McLaurin can improve on the 15.8 FPG (would have ranked ~WR10 last year) he averaged in his most recent healthy season. For one, Kingsbury’s stubbornness and predictability in near-always lining his WR1 up on the left (below) probably meant McLaurin missed out on a lot of efficiency. He saw a +58% increase in his FP/RR on the rare occasions he got to line up on the right side (0.73) compared to on the left (0.46). In contrast, Blough has [pledged to move](https://x.com/DHarrison82/status/2061822055650083044?s=20) McLaurin around the formation more.

As I covered in [*Anatomy of a League Winner*](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/season/2025/anatomy-of-a-league-winner#/) last offseason, first downs per route run (1D/RR) is one of the best ways to spot future league-winning WRs. __So it’s pretty exciting and impressive to me that McLaurin ranked 4th in the NFL in 1D/RR last year (0.135, behind only Puka Nacua, Jaxon Smith-Njigba, and Amon-Ra St. Brown).__ And it becomes even more impressive when you consider that he dealt with the combination of Marcus Mariota and an injured Daniels at QB, Kingsbury hamstringing him from an alignment perspective, and Deebo Samuel (a [Kingsbury wet dream](https://x.com/FantasyPtsData/status/1895988203829555419?s=20)) leading all WRs in designed targets (30), sucking all those opportunities out of the offense. All of that’s been fixed for 2026, making McLaurin yet another middle-round WR target of mine.

I am personally a __Rachaad White__ believer for the reasons I lay out [here](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2026/heaths-favorite-best-ball-values#/) and [here](https://youtu.be/srZ6AIPKQt0?si=dVHBYwOgP9XKsX_N&t=758), for which much of the thesis is that rushing efficiency doesn’t matter. So I’ll instead let Scott Barrett do the heavy lifting below to lay out the upside case for __Jacory Croskey-Merritt__, the most efficient outside zone runner in the NFL last year.

The Commanders ranked 2nd-to-last in outside zone rush attempts in 2025 (66), but [apparently](https://x.com/JPFinlayNBCS/status/2063615477742522496?s=20) want to [use it more](https://commanderswire.usatoday.com/story/sports/nfl/commanders/2026/05/22/washington-commanders-josh-conerly-looks-much-different-2026/90210760007/). And indeed, White is much worse at this; he ranks dead-last of 49 qualifying RBs in outside zone YPC (2.95) over his entire career, compared to more reasonable numbers he’s posted on man/gap (4.52) and inside zone (3.58). If you think Blough will lean toward the more efficient runner rather than the better receiver and pass protector when doling out snaps, this is your argument.
